status: November 17, 2026: complaint v22 (N.D. Cal., 28 pp.) is ready for Plaintiff's review and is not filed. Plaintiff remains employed. His overnight shifts were reduced from 4 to 3 to 2 per week, he received a written warning on Nov. 12, and the Nov. 12 roster restored 3 overnights. Preservation letter and Universal Background Screening file request are drafted and unsent.
key_facts: Sept. 9, 2026: Plaintiff applied through Indeed for the Night Auditor / Guest Service Agent position at Delta Hotels by Marriott Santa Clara–Silicon Valley (2151 Laurelwood Rd., Santa Clara). Sept. 16: in-person interview with John Barros, who later set Plaintiff's schedules. Sept. 22: written offer ($24/hr Night Audit; $23/hr GSA) and a Universal Background Screening packet on the HMG trade name 'Delta Santa Clara'; the authorization recites separate disclosure documents that Plaintiff never received. Sept. 27: Marriott International, Inc. issued Plaintiff's Marriott Enterprise ID. Oct. 9: Marriott verified him for its Explore associate rate. Night Audit training was assigned to Night Auditor Justin Howell. Oct. 29: Howell's 'He released you didn't he?' remark referring to released sex offenders; the Nov. 1–7 roster cutting overnights from 4 to 3 was posted before that shift and photographed Oct. 30 at 7:03 a.m. Nov. 3: Barros texted that he had 'heard' about Plaintiff's attendance. Nov. 5 at 5:52 p.m.: roster cut to 2 overnights. Nov. 11: Howell told Plaintiff the cuts were because he had been calling out. Nov. 12: Barros issued a written warning reciting only Plaintiff's texts to Howell and said the reductions were 'by design'; at 2:02 p.m. he sent a roster restoring 3 overnights. Plaintiff remains employed.
procedural_status: Pre-filing. No complaint, docket, or case number. Complaint v22 (Nov. 17, 2026) incorporates the Nov. 17 Westlaw verification findings (Sessions 1–7). Canonical chronology is clocks.json and events.jsonl.
damages: Lost wages from the shift reductions of about $533–$813 through the week of Nov. 15–21, 2026, plus continuing losses while hours stay reduced; garden-variety emotional distress only. Statutory remedies: § 290.46(j)(4)(A) (actual damages, up to 3× more with a $250 minimum, and exemplary damages or a civil penalty up to $25,000); FCRA § 1681n ($100–$1,000 statutory or actual, plus punitive); ICRAA § 1786.50 (actual or $10,000 per report, whichever is greater, plus punitive if grossly negligent or willful).
risk: Coworker cat's paw is unresolved in the Ninth Circuit and California (Miller v. T-Mobile, N.D. Cal. 2025), and no case applies cat's paw to § 290.46. The attendance record supports an independent-reason defense. FCRA standing in federal court is contested (Gunns, N.D. Cal. 2026); dismissal of the only federal claim ends supplemental jurisdiction (Scott, 9th Cir. 2002), and § 1367(d) tolling after such a dismissal is unsettled. No case holds a franchisor liable for causing a report to be procured; expect a Salazar-based motion by Marriott.
